sectionsContent.title: Unit 5 Test · Day 1: Multiple Choice

concept.summary: Circle the letter of the best answer. Each question is worth 2 points.

items.stem: How many valence electrons go into the Lewis structure of PF₃?
items.why: A counts each F as 1 (its bond). B forgets the P. D gives every atom 8. P 5 + F 7 × 3 = 26.

items.stem: After you COUNT, build the SKELETON and FILL, the central atom has only 6 electrons. What does the CHECK step tell you to do?
options: Turn an outer lone pair into a double bond
Add 2 more electrons to the central atom
Swap the central atom with an outer atom
Leave it; every atom is stable with 6
items.why: B changes the electron total. C treats it as a skeleton error. D stretches the boron exception to every atom.

items.stem: Which atom goes in the center of the Lewis structure for HCN?
options: H, because it is written first
None; a linear molecule has no center
items.why: A: H is never the center atom. C: the least EN atom goes in the center (C 2.55 < N 3.04). D confuses shape with skeleton.

items.stem: According to VSEPR theory, electron pairs around a central atom...
options: spread as far apart as they can
crowd onto one side of the atom
attract each other to form bonds
always sit at 90° in one flat plane
items.why: Slide 13. B and C think the pairs attract. D is the flat-molecule picture.

items.stem: CCl₄ has 109.5° bond angles, but the angles in PCl₃ are less than 109.5°. Why?
options: The lone pair on P repels more strongly and squeezes the bonds closer
P has fewer bonds, so its bonds are shorter
The Cl atoms attract each other
P is more electronegative and pulls the bonds in
items.why: Slide 13 must-write. B confuses length with angle. C puts IMF thinking inside a molecule. D is false (P 2.19 < C 2.55).

items.stem: How many electron groups are on the central C in HCN?
items.why: C counts each pair of the triple bond; a triple bond is ONE group (slide 17). B adds a lone pair C does not have. D also counts N's lone pair.

items.stem: PCl₅ has 5 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs on P. What is its shape?
items.why: A assumes P cannot pass 8. C is the 5 bonds + 1 lone pair shape. D miscounts 6 groups.

items.stem: SO₂ has 2 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair on S. Which pair gives its electron geometry / molecular geometry?
items.why: B swaps the two names. C ignores the lone pair (the CO₂ habit). D counts 4 groups.

items.stem: BCl₃ has three polar B–Cl bonds (ΔEN 1.12), but the molecule is nonpolar. Why?
options: The three equal dipoles are spread symmetrically and cancel
Bonds between nonmetals are always nonpolar
B has only 6 electrons, so no dipole forms
The lone pairs on Cl cancel the dipoles
items.why: B equates bond type with polarity. C mixes up the octet exception with polarity. D thinks outer lone pairs decide polarity.
A and B: polar bonds, but symmetric, so they cancel. D: same atoms, ΔEN 0. PCl₃'s lone pair makes it a pyramid, so the pulls add.

items.stem: For the H–Cl bond, which way does the dipole arrow point?
options: Toward H, because it has fewer electrons
Both ways; HCl has no direction
items.why: Slide 10: the arrow points toward δ−, cross at δ+. B and C reverse it. D ignores the partial charges.

items.stem: When a molecular liquid boils, what is overcome?
options: Lone pairs on the central atom
items.why: Slide 32: bonds hold a molecule together; IMFs hold molecules to each other. B and D confuse intramolecular with intermolecular.

items.stem: Which substance can form hydrogen bonds with other molecules of itself?
items.why: A has H, but it is on Cl. B has H on C. C has F but no H. Slide 33: H on N, O, or F.

items.stem: Which intermolecular force is present in every molecule?
items.why: Slide 35: every molecule. A is the strongest, not the most common. B needs a polar molecule. D is a bond, not an IMF.

items.stem: F₂ and Cl₂ are gases, Br₂ is a liquid and I₂ is a solid at room temperature. What explains this trend?
options: More electrons give stronger London dispersion forces
The I–I bond is the strongest bond
items.why: Slide 35: bigger = stronger, I₂ is a solid. A: all are nonpolar (ΔEN 0). B: no H. D confuses the bond inside the molecule with IMFs.

keyNotes: No question uses a Day 2 chart molecule, so Day 1 does not hand out Day 2 answers.
